interactions.label: In the DRSABC primary assessment, Airway is checked before Circulation. Which of

params.question: In the DRSABC primary assessment, Airway is checked before Circulation. Which of the following best explains the reasoning behind this order?

answers.text: Airway equipment is simpler to use and more widely available than circulatory support devices

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The order is based on how quickly each problem kills, not on equipment availability. A blocked airway causes death faster than circulatory failure.

answers.text: A blocked airway kills in minutes — faster than most circulatory failures — so the most rapidly lethal problem is addressed first

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The DRSABC sequence follows a time-to-death hierarchy: airway obstruction kills fastest, then absent breathing, then circulatory failure. Each step addresses the most immediately lethal threat before moving on.

answers.text: Circulatory assessment requires two rescuers, whereas airway management can be done alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both airway and circulatory assessment can be performed by a single rescuer. The ordering principle is the speed at which each problem kills, not the number of hands required.

answers.text: Airway obstruction is the most common injury in road traffic accidents

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sequence is ordered by time-to-death, not by injury frequency. A blocked airway kills in minutes regardless of how common it is relative to other injuries.

overallFeedback.feedback: The DRSABC sequence follows a time-to-death hierarchy: airway obstruction kills fastest, then absent breathing, then circulatory failure. Each step addresses the most immediately lethal problem first.
Correct! The DRSABC sequence is ordered by how rapidly each problem kills — a blocked airway causes death in minutes, so it is addressed before circulatory problems.

params.question: An unresponsive adult is found making slow, irregular, snoring gasps. You have called for help and sent for an AED. What is the correct next action?

answers.text: Place the casualty in the recovery position and reassess every two minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The recovery position is for an unresponsive casualty who IS breathing normally. Agonal gasps are not normal breathing — they signal cardiac arrest and require immediate chest compressions.

answers.text: Perform a head-tilt chin-lift and wait one minute to see if breathing improves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting wastes critical time. In cardiac arrest, survival falls with every passing minute. Once agonal gasps are recognised, compressions must begin without delay.

answers.text: Start chest compressions at 100–120 per minute in the centre of the chest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Agonal gasps — slow, irregular, snoring breaths — signal cardiac arrest, not life. Begin compressions immediately: 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 per minute, with full recoil, in cycles of 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

answers.text: Check the carotid pulse for up to thirty seconds before deciding on compressions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Never delay compressions to check for a pulse when breathing is absent or abnormal. The video explicitly states this rule — start compressions immediately.

overallFeedback.feedback: Agonal gasps — slow, irregular, snoring breaths — are not normal breathing. They signal cardiac arrest. The correct response is to start chest compressions immediately at 100–120 per minute, never delaying to check for a pulse.
Correct! Agonal gasps signal cardiac arrest. Begin chest compressions immediately at 100–120 per minute, 5–6 cm deep, without delaying for a pulse check.

interactions.label: Dozens of casualties arrive after a bus overturn. Why does the video warn agains

params.question: Dozens of casualties arrive after a bus overturn. Why does the video warn against rushing to treat the most dramatically injured patient first?

answers.text: Severely injured patients are beyond saving in a field setting and should only receive comfort care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not all severely injured patients are unsaveable. The warning is about resource allocation: focusing everything on one patient means others with survivable injuries go untreated.

answers.text: Focusing all resources on one patient means others with survivable injuries go untreated and may die

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When casualties overwhelm resources, directing all care to one dramatic case causes more total deaths. The governing principle becomes 'the greatest good for the greatest number' — triage ensures resources reach those most likely to benefit.

answers.text: Dramatic injuries are usually superficial and do not require immediate medical intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dramatic injuries can be genuinely life-threatening. The issue is not their severity but the allocation of limited resources — treating one patient exclusively leaves many others to die.

answers.text: Emergency protocols mandate treating patients strictly in order of arrival at the facility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no arrival-order protocol. In a mass casualty incident, triage sorts patients by urgency and likelihood of benefit from treatment, not by when they arrived.

overallFeedback.feedback: When casualties overwhelm resources, treating only the most dramatic case means others with survivable injuries go untreated and die. Triage — sorting by urgency and survivability — replaces the instinct to rush to the worst case first.
Correct! In mass casualty incidents, directing all resources to the most dramatic case costs lives elsewhere. Triage ensures the greatest good for the greatest number.

interactions.label: During START triage, a non-ambulant casualty has a respiratory rate of 22 per mi

params.question: During START triage, a non-ambulant casualty has a respiratory rate of 22 per minute, a palpable radial pulse, and follows your simple verbal command. What colour tag should this casualty receive?

answers.text: Green (minor) — the casualty's vital signs are within normal limits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Green is reserved for casualties who can walk. The walking filter is the first step in START — anyone who cannot walk proceeds to RPM assessment regardless of vital signs.

answers.text: Red (immediate) — all non-ambulant casualties require immediate intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-ambulant casualties are not automatically red. They must meet at least one RPM criterion: respiratory rate above 30, absent radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds, or inability to follow a simple command.

answers.text: Yellow (delayed) — breathing, perfusion, and mental status are adequate but the casualty cannot walk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Apply START step by step: cannot walk → assess RPM. Respiratory rate 22 (under the 30/min threshold), radial pulse present (perfusion adequate), follows commands (mental status intact). No red criteria are met, so the tag is yellow — delayed but not immediately life-threatening.

answers.text: Black (expectant) — the casualty is on the ground and not moving independently

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Black is only for casualties who are not breathing even after the airway is opened. Being unable to walk does not make a casualty expectant — that requires absent breathing after airway intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Apply the START algorithm step by step. Non-ambulant → check RPM. Respiratory rate 22 (under 30 threshold), radial pulse present (perfusion adequate), follows commands (mental status intact). No red criteria met — the correct tag is yellow (delayed).
Correct! START triage: non-ambulant → check RPM. Respiratory rate under 30, radial pulse present, follows commands — no red criteria met. The tag is yellow (delayed).
